center.note: Plans phases, keeps its context small

spokes.label: Focused subagents
spokes.note: Read a lot, return short summaries

quiz.q: You need a list of every test file that touches refunds in a 2,000-file repo. How should the main agent get it?
options: Delegate it to a subagent that returns only the file paths
Read every test file itself so it has the complete picture
Ask the user to paste the relevant test files into the chat
Rely on what it remembers from reading files earlier on
quiz.why: A focused subagent does the reading in its own context and returns a short list, keeping the coordinator's context small.

quiz.q: A developer suggests the main agent read all of `src/` upfront "to get the full picture". What is the main problem?
options: Subagents cannot read files the main agent has already opened
The model cannot read more than a few hundred files in total
It uses up the main context before any real work can start
Claude Code blocks bulk reads unless plan mode is switched on
quiz.why: Reading everything fills the main context with raw file contents. Targeted subagent questions return only the summaries the coordinator needs.

quiz.q: Which practice keeps early findings usable after the context is compacted or a new session begins?
options: Repeating the findings in the prompt at the start of each turn
Writing key findings, with exact names, to scratchpad files
Asking the model to try harder to remember earlier findings
Switching to plan mode for the remainder of the exploration
quiz.why: Files survive context boundaries; the model's working memory does not. Written notes can be reloaded at any time.

quiz.q: Late in an exploration, answers start drifting. The team plans to add "remember everything you found earlier" to the prompt. What is better?
options: Make the reminder louder by repeating it in capital letters
Use a longer system prompt with more detailed instructions
Restart the session and re-read every file from the beginning
Persist findings to files, delegate questions, pass summaries
quiz.why: Degradation is structural, so prompt wording will not fix it. Files, subagents and phase summaries change how context is used.

misconceptions.myth: Subagents can see what the coordinator has already found.
misconceptions.fact: They start with a fresh context. Inject the previous phase's summary into their prompts explicitly.

misconceptions.myth: Context problems only appear when the window is completely full.
misconceptions.fact: Quality degrades gradually. Vague, generic or inconsistent answers are the early warning.

misconceptions.myth: Reading everything upfront gives the agent the best understanding.
misconceptions.fact: It exhausts the main context. Targeted subagent questions return only what is needed.

scenario.title: Code Generation with Claude Code
scenario.story:
A developer asked Claude Code to work out how refunds flow through a 2,000-file legacy codebase and then add partial refunds. Early on, the agent correctly spotted that `RefundLedgerService` was the live class and `RefundService` was legacy.

Two hours and 300 files later, she asked which class writes refund entries. The answer was 'typically a RefundService or repository layer'. Asked again, it gave a third answer. The context was full of raw file contents, and the early finding had faded.

She restructured the work. A subagent found the entry point and returned paths only. The main agent wrote `notes/phase1-summary.md` with exact class names, and updated `state/manifest.json`. A second subagent, given that summary in its prompt, listed the six callers of `RefundLedgerService`. When the terminal crashed halfway through, the coordinator reloaded the manifest and the notes and resumed at phase two. She used `/compact` once the session grew long. The final plan named exact files and methods, with no drift.

currentNote: The exam calls the subagent-spawning tool `Task`. In current Claude Code it is named `Agent` (renamed in v2.1.63), so hooks or log checks that match on the tool name should accept both.

plain: Before letting a model extract data from documents without a human checking, you need to know where it is actually reliable. A headline figure like "97% accurate" can hide one document type or one field that is often wrong. So measure accuracy per document type and per field, set review thresholds using real labelled data, and send only the doubtful items to people.
analogy: A school might boast a 97% pass rate, but that could hide one subject where half the class fails. You would not stop checking that subject's marks just because the average looks great.

sections.body:
**A high overall accuracy can hide a weak document type or a weak field.**

Suppose an extraction pipeline is **97% accurate** across 10,000 documents. It sounds ready to automate. But break it down:

- invoices: 99.4%
- contracts: 98.8%
- scanned receipts: 79%, and the `total` field on receipts only 71%

Receipts are a small share of the volume, so the average hides them. If you automate everything, hundreds of wrong receipt totals get paid out.

This lesson is about knowing **where** the model is reliable before you remove human checks. That means measuring by segment, using field-level confidence, calibrating thresholds on real data, and spending limited reviewer time where errors actually are.

sections.h: Measure by document type and field
sections.body:
**Validate each segment separately, using documents whose correct answers you already know.**

1. **Build a labelled validation set.** These are documents where a person has recorded the correct value for every field. Cover every document type you expect in production.
2. **Run the pipeline on it** and compare each extracted field with the label.
3. **Break accuracy down** by document type (invoice, receipt, contract) and by field (supplier, date, total).
4. **Find the weak cells**, such as receipt totals or handwritten dates.
5. **Automate only the segments** that meet your accuracy bar. Keep the rest under human review until they improve.

This is **stratified** measurement: looking at each layer of the data on its own rather than one blended average.

**Score each field, then set cut-offs from labelled data rather than by feel.**

Ask the model to return a **confidence per field** in its structured output, for example `{"total": {"value": "48.20", "confidence": 0.71}}`. One score for the whole document hides which value is shaky, so reviewers must re-check everything.

Then **calibrate** a threshold for each document type and field:

1. On the labelled set, look at the real error rate at each confidence level.
2. Pick the lowest confidence at which errors are acceptable for that field.
3. Fields below it go to review.

The result might be 0.92 for receipt totals but 0.85 for invoice totals. A round 0.8 chosen by intuition could still let through a 12% error rate on dates.

**Send humans only the doubtful items, and keep sampling the rest.**

Route to the limited reviewer capacity:

- **low-confidence fields**, with the field highlighted
- **ambiguous or contradictory documents**, for example line items that do not add up to the stated total, even if each field looks confident

Everything else is auto-approved, but not forgotten. Take a **stratified random sample** of high-confidence extractions, a small share from each document type, and have reviewers check it. This measures their real error rate and catches **new error patterns**, such as a new supplier's date format.

What goes wrong: automating on the aggregate figure, one document-level score, untested round-number thresholds, and stopping review of high-confidence items once thresholds are set.

example.title: Worked example: field-level confidence and per-field thresholds
notes: Each field carries its own confidence, so reviewers see exactly which value is doubtful.
Thresholds differ per document type and per field because they were calibrated on labelled data, not chosen by feel.
The receipt date at 0.93 is routed for review because receipts needed 0.95 to reach an acceptable error rate.
A contradiction (line items do not sum to the total) sends the document to a human regardless of confidence.
Items marked `auto` are still randomly sampled for QA to measure their real error rate.

labs.title: 97% overall accuracy: ready to automate?
labs.context: Your extraction pipeline scores 97% accuracy overall on a 10,000-document labelled set of invoices, receipts and contracts. Reviewers can check about 400 items a day, and the business wants to stop reviewing what the model handles well. Errors that reach payment are costly, so the plan must not hide a weak document type or field.
labs.question: Which rollout plan should the team adopt?

options.text: Automate all three document types now, since 97% accuracy on a 10,000-document labelled set is a large and representative sample.
options.code:
rollout:
  mode: full_auto
  justification: "97% overall accuracy on test set"
  human_review: none

trace.text: All 10,000 documents processed with no review.
Breakdown nobody ran: invoices 99.4%, contracts 98.8%, receipts 79% (total field 71%).
Week 2: finance finds 230 receipts with wrong totals already paid out.
How did 97% accuracy produce this many bad payments?

options.verdict: The aggregate hid a weak document type and a weak field.
options.why: Aggregate accuracy can mask poor performance on a specific document type or field. Trap: a big sample size does not replace a per-type, per-field breakdown.

options.text: Validate accuracy per document type and field, calibrate field-level thresholds on the labelled set, route low-confidence fields to reviewers, and keep sampling.
options.code:
validation: per_doc_type_and_field   # labelled set
confidence: per_field
thresholds: calibrated_on_labelled_set
route_to_human:
  - low_confidence_fields
  - contradictory_or_ambiguous_docs
qa_sampling:
  strategy: stratified_random
  rate: 2%   # of auto-approved, per doc type

trace.text: Validation by segment: invoices and contracts pass; receipt totals fail at the default level.
Calibrated thresholds: receipt.total needs 0.92; invoice.total 0.85.
Daily: 9,600 fields auto-approved; 310 low-confidence fields plus 60 contradictory docs routed to reviewers.
Reviewers see the flagged field highlighted and clear the queue within capacity.
Stratified sample catches a new supplier date format in week 3; threshold for that segment tightened.

options.verdict: Reviewer time goes where errors are, and new error patterns get caught.
options.why: Measure and calibrate per document type and per field, send only low-confidence or contradictory items to humans, and keep sampling the rest.

options.text: Use one document-level confidence score with a 0.8 review cut-off, sending only documents that score below 0.8 to the reviewers.
options.code:
rollout:
  confidence: per_document
  review_if_below: 0.8   # round number, untested
  sample_high_confidence: false

trace.text: Receipt #5521: document confidence 0.86 (total field was the shaky part).
0.86 >= 0.8, auto-approved.
Receipt #6002: confidence 0.78, sent to reviewer with no hint which field is wrong.
Reviewer re-checks all 14 fields; throughput drops to 150 a day.
New supplier format starts causing confident date errors; with no sampling, nobody notices.

options.verdict: Review is aimed blindly: weak fields slip through and reviewers recheck whole documents.
options.why: A document score hides which field is uncertain, an untested 0.8 does not match real error rates, and without sampling new error patterns go unseen. Trap: a threshold that looks calibrated but never was.

options.text: Have the model re-check each extraction against the source in a second pass, and automate only the documents where both passes agree.
options.code:
rollout:
  self_check: second_pass
  auto_approve_if: passes_agree
  human_review: disagreements_only

trace.text: Second pass agrees with the first on 96% of receipts.
Both passes misread tip lines as part of the total in the same way.
210 receipts with wrong totals auto-approved.
Reviewers only saw disagreements, and none of these were among them.

options.verdict: Agreement looked like accuracy, but both passes shared the same blind spot.
options.why: Two passes by the same model share its systematic errors, so agreement is not a measured error rate. Trap: probabilistic self-checking instead of validation against labelled data.

labs.takeaway: Break accuracy down by type and field, calibrate thresholds on labelled data, and keep sampling what you automate.

labs.title: Auto-posting review findings above a confidence bar
labs.context: Your CI pipeline runs Claude Code on every pull request, and 91% of 1,200 labelled past findings were valid overall. The team now wants to auto-post findings above a confidence threshold and send the rest to one reviewer, who can triage about 40 a day. Developers have said they will mute the bot if its security findings keep being wrong.
labs.question: What should the team do before turning on auto-posting?

options.text: Auto-post every finding now, since 91% validity across 1,200 labelled findings is strong evidence that the reviewer step adds little.

trace.text: Breakdown nobody ran: style 98%, performance 90%, security 58% valid.
Week 1: 19 false security alarms posted on pull requests.
Developers mute the bot on three repositories.

options.verdict: The aggregate hid the one category developers care most about.
options.why: Aggregate accuracy can mask a weak category, and here it hid the security findings. Trap: treating one overall figure as permission to automate everything.

options.text: Add an instruction to the review prompt telling Claude to report only findings it is highly confident about, and auto-post all of them.
options.code:
Only report findings you are highly confident
are real problems. Skip anything uncertain.

trace.text: Findings per pull request drop from 30 to 18.
Security findings are still only 60% valid.
Reviewer queue is empty; nothing is measured.

options.verdict: Fewer findings, same weak security precision, and no measurement at all.
options.why: Self-reported confidence is not calibrated, so the filter cuts volume without targeting errors. Trap: a probabilistic instruction where measured, calibrated thresholds are needed.

options.text: Auto-post findings whose confidence exceeds 0.8, the value the team agreed matches 'high confidence' in its existing review guidelines.
options.code:
auto_post:
  min_confidence: 0.8   # agreed in guidelines, untested
below_threshold: route_to_reviewer

trace.text: At 0.8, security findings are 64% valid on the labelled set nobody checked.
Style findings at 0.6-0.8 are 97% valid, yet all are queued.
Reviewer receives about 120 findings a day against a capacity of 40.

options.verdict: Wrong findings still posted, right ones queued, reviewer swamped.
options.why: A threshold picked by agreement rather than calibration does not match real error rates per category. Trap: a number that sounds principled but was never tested.

options.text: Measure precision per finding category on the labelled set, calibrate a threshold for each category, and route below-threshold findings to the reviewer.
options.code:
auto_post:
  thresholds:          # calibrated on 1,200 labelled findings
    style: 0.55
    performance: 0.80
    security: 0.95
  below_threshold: route_to_reviewer
qa_sample: 3%          # of auto-posted, stratified by category

trace.text: Labelled set by category: style 98%, performance 90%, security 58% valid.
Thresholds calibrated per category; about 35 findings a day routed to the reviewer.
Auto-posted security findings now 96% valid.
Developers keep the bot switched on.

options.verdict: Trustworthy auto-posts, and the reviewer's 40 slots go where errors are.
options.why: Validate by category before automating, and calibrate thresholds on labelled data rather than intuition. Limited reviewer time then goes to the findings most likely to be wrong.

labs.takeaway: Before automating, break precision down by category and calibrate a threshold for each on labelled data.

labs.title: Fact-checkers never see high-confidence claims
labs.context: Your research system attaches a calibrated confidence score to each claim, auto-publishes claims above 0.9, and sends the rest (about 38 a day) to fact-checkers who can handle 50. Since the system began citing preprint servers, readers have reported three wrong statistics, all from auto-published claims. The team cannot hire more fact-checkers.
labs.question: What change best catches errors like these?

options.text: Each day, send fact-checkers a random sample of auto-published claims, stratified by source type, to measure error rates and catch new error patterns.
options.code:
review_queue:
  below_threshold: all          # ~38/day
  qa_sample:
    from: auto_published
    strategy: stratified_random
    strata: [journal, preprint, government, news]
    per_stratum_per_day: 3       # ~12/day

trace.text: Day 2: sample includes 3 preprint claims; 2 are wrong (figures revised in later versions).
Measured error rate: preprints 31%, journals 2%.
Preprint threshold recalibrated to 0.97; most preprint claims now reviewed.
Reader-reported errors stop; checkers stay within 50 a day.

options.verdict: The new error pattern was measured within days, within existing capacity.
options.why: Stratified random sampling of high-confidence output is how error rates are measured and novel patterns found. Stratifying by source type exposed the weak segment the overall rate hid.

options.text: Raise the auto-publish threshold from 0.9 to 0.97 for every claim, so that a much larger share of claims goes through fact-checking.
options.code:
auto_publish:
  min_confidence: 0.97   # was 0.9, all source types
review_queue:
  below_threshold: all

trace.text: Review queue jumps from 38 to 210 claims a day.
Checkers clear 50; reports are delayed by a week.
Some wrong preprint claims still score 0.98 and publish.

options.verdict: Capacity overwhelmed, and the weak segment still slipped through.
options.why: A blanket threshold change is not targeted and blows through the stated review capacity. Without measurement, you do not know which segment needs a stricter bar.

options.text: Remove preprint servers from the sources the web-search subagent may use, since that is where every reported error so far has come from.

trace.text: Preprints excluded from search.
Reports lose coverage of the most recent research.
Month 2: errors from machine-translated government PDFs are auto-published; nobody notices.

options.verdict: This one source is gone, but the next novel error pattern is just as invisible.
options.why: Right pattern, wrong problem: it removes one symptom and coverage with it, but adds no way to measure high-confidence errors. Ongoing sampling is what catches the next pattern.

options.text: Add a self-check step in which the synthesis agent re-verifies each high-confidence claim against its source before the claim is published.

trace.text: Re-checks the claim against preprint v1: the figure matches.
The figure was revised in v2; the claim is still wrong.
Self-check passes 99.6% of claims; no error rate is measured.

options.verdict: The check confirmed the error instead of catching it.
options.why: Self-verification checks a claim against the same source the model already relied on and produces no measured error rate. Trap: probabilistic self-review where human sampling is needed.

labs.takeaway: Keep a stratified random sample of high-confidence output under human review; it is how you see errors the scores miss.

checks.q: Why is a 97% overall accuracy figure not enough to justify full automation?
checks.a: It can hide a document type or field with a much higher error rate. Break accuracy down by type and field first.

checks.q: What is the advantage of field-level confidence over one document-level score?
checks.a: It shows which specific field is uncertain, so reviewers focus on the value most likely to be wrong.

checks.q: Once thresholds are set, why keep sampling high-confidence extractions?
checks.a: Stratified random sampling measures their real error rate and catches new error patterns that thresholds alone would miss.

steps.note: Known answers for every document type

steps.label: Stratify accuracy
steps.note: Break down by type and field

steps.label: Calibrate thresholds
steps.note: Per field, against the labelled data

steps.label: Field above threshold?
steps.note: And no contradictions in the document

quiz.q: How should the team choose the confidence threshold below which a field goes to human review?
options: Use 0.8 for every field, since it is a common default
Use the average confidence the model gave on the test set
Calibrate it per field against a labelled validation set
Let reviewers adjust it each day based on how busy they are
quiz.why: Thresholds must be tested against labelled data so they match real error rates. A round number chosen by intuition may not.

quiz.q: Reviewers can check about 400 items a day. Which items should reach them?
options: A random selection of all documents processed that day
Every document from the highest-volume document type
All documents with an overall confidence under 0.9
Low-confidence fields and contradictory or ambiguous documents
quiz.why: Limited reviewer time goes where errors are most likely. Field-level routing also tells reviewers exactly which value to check.

quiz.q: Validation shows invoices at 99% accuracy, receipts at 79%, and 97% overall. What is the sensible next step?
options: Automate invoices only, and keep receipts under human review
Automate everything, since 97% overall is above the target
Automate receipts first, as they need the most attention
Delay all automation until the overall figure reaches 99%
quiz.why: Automate only the segments that are validated as reliable. The weak segment stays under review until it improves.

quiz.q: How should high-confidence, auto-approved extractions be checked over time?
options: Not at all, since their confidence is already above threshold
A stratified random sample from each document type, reviewed
Only the first week of output after launch, then stop
Only those from the document type with the largest volume
quiz.why: Stratified sampling measures the real error rate of auto-approved items in every segment and catches new error patterns early.

misconceptions.myth: A high confidence score means the field is correct.
misconceptions.fact: Confidence is only useful once it has been calibrated against labelled data. Uncalibrated scores can be confidently wrong.

misconceptions.myth: Once thresholds are set, high-confidence items no longer need review.
misconceptions.fact: Keep a stratified random sample under review to measure real error rates and catch new error patterns.

misconceptions.myth: One confidence score per document is enough to route reviews.
misconceptions.fact: It hides which field is uncertain. Field-level scores let reviewers check the right value.

scenario.title: Structured Data Extraction
scenario.story:
A finance team built a pipeline to extract supplier, date and total from invoices, receipts and contracts. On their test set it scored **97% overall**, so they switched off human review. Two weeks later, accounts payable found 230 receipts paid at the wrong amount.

The team went back to the labelled set and broke accuracy down. Invoices were 99.4% and contracts 98.8%, but scanned receipts were 79%, and the receipt `total` field was only 71%. The average had hidden it.

They changed the output to give a confidence score per field. Using the labelled set, they calibrated thresholds for each document type and field: receipt totals needed 0.92, invoice totals 0.85. Low-confidence fields, and any document whose line items did not add up to the total, went to the four reviewers with the doubtful field highlighted. A 2% stratified sample of auto-approved items was also reviewed each day. In week three that sample caught a new supplier date format, and the team tightened that segment's threshold.

plain: A research report built from many sources is only trustworthy if each claim can be traced back to where it came from. When sources disagree, the report should show both views with their sources, not quietly pick one. Dates matter too, because two different numbers may just come from different years.
analogy: A good recipe book credits each recipe and notes when two cooks disagree on the oven temperature. A bad one blends every version into one recipe with no names, so when the cake burns you cannot tell whose advice to trust.

sections.body:
**Every claim in a report should carry its own source, excerpt and date.**

**Provenance** means knowing where each claim came from. In a multi-agent research system, subagents gather findings and a synthesis step writes the report. Attribution is easily lost on the way, especially when findings are compressed into short prose.

The fix is a **claim-source mapping**: a small structured record for each finding with:

- the **claim** itself, and the value if it is a number
- the **source**: a URL or document name
- a short **excerpt** in the source's own words
- the **publication or collection date**
- useful **methodology** notes, such as sample size

Subagents output these mappings instead of paragraphs. Once attribution is dropped upstream, no later step can reconstruct it.

**The synthesis step may reorganise claims, but it must never strip their sources.**

1. **Subagents return structured mappings**, one per claim.
2. **The coordinator reviews them** and flags conflicts before synthesis begins. It decides how to handle each one, for example by presenting both values or sending a subagent to check methodology.
3. **Synthesis preserves and merges** the mappings. It can group claims by theme and remove duplicates, but every claim in the report keeps its citation.
4. **The report separates well-established findings from contested ones**, and keeps each source's own wording and context.

A 'stronger synthesis prompt' cannot replace this. If the mappings never reached the synthesis step, the prompt has nothing to cite.

**Show disagreements with attribution, and check dates before calling anything a conflict.**

When two credible sources give different figures, do **not** pick the most plausible one. Report both, each with its source, and mark the point as contested. For example: '44% (SME Tech Survey, June 2024, 1,200 firms) vs 61% (Vendor Report, March 2024, existing customers only).'

Before treating two numbers as a conflict, check:

- **Dates.** 12% in 2022 and 18% in 2024 may be a trend, not a contradiction.
- **Methodology.** One survey may count only large firms, another all firms.

This is why dates and methods belong in the structured output. Without them, a change over time looks like two sources arguing.

sections.h: Formatting by content type, and common mistakes
sections.body:
**Present each kind of content in the format that suits it.**

- **Financial and numeric data:** tables, so figures can be compared at a glance.
- **News and developments:** prose, which carries sequence and context.
- **Technical findings:** lists, which are easy to scan.

Flattening everything into uniform bullet points looks tidy but makes comparisons harder to read.

Common mistakes:

- Synthesis **quietly picks** one figure when sources disagree.
- Subagents return **concise prose** to save context, and attribution disappears.
- A **time difference** is treated as a contradiction because dates were not captured.
- **Methodological context** is stripped, so incomparable numbers look comparable.
- The team tries to fix missing citations with a **stronger synthesis prompt**.

example.title: Worked example: a subagent's claim-source mappings with a conflict
example.code:
{
  "topic": "UK SME cloud adoption rate",
  "claims": [
    {
      "claim": "44% of UK SMEs use at least one cloud accounting tool",
      "value": 0.44,
      "source": "https://example.org/sme-tech-survey-2024",
      "document": "SME Tech Survey 2024",
      "excerpt": "44% of respondents reported using cloud accounting software",
      "published": "2024-06",
      "methodology": "online survey, 1,200 firms, 10-249 staff"
    },
    {
      "claim": "61% of UK SMEs use cloud accounting",
      "value": 0.61,
      "source": "https://example.com/vendor-report",
      "document": "Vendor Market Report",
      "excerpt": "Six in ten small businesses now run their books in the cloud",
      "published": "2024-03",
      "methodology": "customer panel, existing software users only"
    }
  ],
  "conflicts": [{"claims": [0, 1], "note": "Same period; different sampling frames"}]
}
notes: Each claim carries its own source, document name and verbatim excerpt, so synthesis can cite it directly.
`published` dates show these figures are from the same period, so this is a real disagreement rather than a trend.
`methodology` keeps the context that explains the gap: one panel only includes existing software users.
`conflicts` flags the disagreement for the coordinator to decide on before synthesis, instead of picking a winner.
The final report would present both figures with attribution, and could put them in a table since they are numeric.

labs.title: Two credible sources disagree on adoption
labs.context: Two credible subagent findings give different figures, 44% and 61%, for SME cloud-accounting adoption in the same year. The coordinator must produce a board-ready report, and the board will size an investment on this number. Every figure in the report must be traceable to its source.
labs.question: How should findings flow from the subagents into synthesis?

options.text: Have the synthesis agent choose the more plausible of the two figures, so the board receives one clear number rather than a confusing range.
options.code:
Synthesis prompt:
"Combine the findings below into a clean report.
Where numbers conflict, use the most plausible one
so the report reads clearly."

trace.text: Subagent A: 44% (survey, 2024). Subagent B: 61% (vendor panel, 2024).
Synthesis judges 61% more plausible and writes: "61% of UK SMEs use cloud accounting."
Board approves a plan sized on 61% penetration.
Later review: 61% came from a panel of existing software customers only; independent survey said 44%.

options.verdict: A real disagreement was hidden and the board acted on a biased number.
options.why: Silently choosing one figure hides a real disagreement between credible sources. Trap: resolving a conflict in synthesis instead of annotating both values with attribution.

options.text: Ask subagents for 2-3 sentence prose summaries to save context, and leave the synthesis agent to reconcile the conflicting figures.
options.code:
# no sources, dates or excerpts requested
Subagent prompt:
"Summarise what you found in 2-3 sentences.
Keep it short to save context."

trace.text: Subagent A: 'Cloud accounting adoption among SMEs is in the 40-60% range according to recent research.'
Subagent B: 'Most small businesses now use cloud accounting.'
Synthesis writes: "Around half to most SMEs use cloud accounting [sources: various]."
Which source says 60%? Is that this year or older?
Cannot tell; source names and dates were not passed through.

options.verdict: The report cannot be verified; attribution and dates were lost upstream.
options.why: Compressed prose without claim-source mappings loses attribution that synthesis cannot reconstruct, no matter how good the synthesis prompt is.

options.text: Have subagents return claim-source mappings with dates and methodology; the coordinator flags the conflict and the report shows both figures with attribution.
options.code:
Subagent output: JSON claims with source, excerpt,
published date, methodology.
Coordinator: flags conflict before synthesis.
Synthesis: preserve mappings; show both values with
attribution; numeric data as a table.

trace.text: Subagents return claim-source mappings with dates and methodology.
Coordinator: same period, different samples. Decision: present both, explain the difference.
Report table: 44% (SME Tech Survey, Jun 2024, 1,200 firms) vs 61% (Vendor Report, Mar 2024, existing customers only).
Report marks adoption rate as 'contested'; other findings marked 'well established'.
Board sizes the plan on a range and asks for one more independent source.

options.verdict: Every claim is traceable and the disagreement is visible, so the decision is informed.
options.why: Carry structured claim-source mappings with dates end to end, and surface conflicts with attribution instead of resolving them silently.

options.text: Add 'cite a source for every claim and figure' to the synthesis prompt, so the finished board report carries citations throughout.
options.code:
Write the board report from the findings below.
Cite a source for every claim and every number.

trace.text: Subagent prose: 'adoption is in the 40-60% range according to recent research'.
Synthesis writes '61% [Industry sources, 2024]'.
Which industry source? I cannot find it.
The source names were not in the findings provided.

options.verdict: The report looks cited, but the citations cannot be traced.
options.why: Synthesis cannot cite what the subagents never passed on, so it generalises or guesses. Trap: a prompt fix at the wrong stage; attribution must travel as structured mappings from the start.

labs.takeaway: Claim-source mappings travel end to end, and conflicts are shown with attribution, not resolved silently.

labs.title: Headcount 'conflicts' that are really different dates
labs.context: Your pipeline extracts company facts such as headcount and revenue from annual reports, press releases and filings, merging them into one record per company. It flags 38% of records as 'contradictory' and routes them to two reviewers, who find most are simply figures from different years. Reviewers can handle only about a tenth of the current flagged volume.
labs.question: Which schema change best reduces the false contradictions?

options.text: Extract each value with its source document and its as-of or publication date, and treat values as conflicting only when they cover the same period.

trace.text: Extracts 4,200 (annual report, as of 2023-12-31) and 4,850 (filing, as of 2024-12-31).
Different periods: stored as a time series, not flagged.
Flagged records fall from 38% to 3%.
Reviewers now see only same-period conflicts, within capacity.

options.verdict: Most "contradictions" turned into a dated history; real conflicts still reach people.
options.why: Including publication or as-of dates stops differences over time being misread as contradictions. Keeping the source per value preserves attribution for the genuine conflicts.

options.text: Keep one value per field, taking the figure from the most recently published source document, so that every company record holds a single clean answer.

trace.text: 2025 press release says 'over 4,000 staff', quoting an old figure.
Most recent document wins: headcount = 4,000.
The 2024 filing said 4,850; the newer, correct figure is discarded.

options.verdict: Fewer flags, but a stale figure won because its document was newer.
options.why: Publication date is not the date a figure describes, and picking one value silently drops attribution. Trap: resolving conflicts by rule instead of recording what each source says and when.

options.text: Instruct the model to ignore small differences between sources and record the figure that most of the source documents agree on.
options.code:
If sources give different values for a field,
ignore small differences and record the value
most sources agree on.

trace.text: Three old documents say 4,200; one recent filing says 4,850.
Records 4,200, the majority value.
The record is now wrong and shows no sign of disagreement.

options.verdict: The flags fell because the evidence was hidden, not because it was understood.
options.why: Majority voting across documents from different years favours older, repeated figures and hides real disagreement. Trap: smoothing over conflicts instead of dating and attributing them.

options.text: Add a reconciliation subagent that reads every source document for each flagged record and decides which of the figures is correct.

trace.text: Reconciliation subagent reads 6 documents per flagged record.
Picks 4,850 for one company and an older figure for a similar case.
Processing cost doubles; decisions are inconsistent and unexplained.

options.verdict: Expensive, inconsistent, and the dates that explain the difference are still missing.
options.why: Over-engineered: a new agent is added before the proportionate schema fix of capturing dates. It also resolves conflicts silently instead of showing both values with attribution.

labs.takeaway: Put dates and sources on every extracted value, so differences over time are not mistaken for contradictions.

labs.title: Upgrade briefing flattens everything into bullets
labs.context: Your internal Agent SDK tool combines three subagents (changelog reader, vulnerability-database search and codebase grep) into a briefing on upgrading a core framework. Synthesis renders everything as one flat bullet list, so engineers cannot compare versions, fixes and severities, and a vendor's 'possible' breaking change reads like a confirmed one. Each finding already arrives with its source and date.
labs.question: What change should the team make to the synthesis step?

options.text: Render the whole briefing as structured JSON, so every finding has the same predictable shape for both engineers and downstream tools.

trace.text: Produces 140 uniform JSON findings.
Which version closes the most CVEs? I have to scroll through 140 objects.
'Possible' breaking change still stored as plain text 'Session API changes'.

options.verdict: A different flat format, still unreadable for comparison and still losing the hedge.
options.why: One uniform format, whatever it is, still flattens content types that read best differently. It also does nothing to keep each source's original characterisation.

options.text: Ask the synthesis agent to write shorter, more concise bullets, with the most important findings placed at the top of the list for quick scanning.

trace.text: List shrinks from 140 to 60 bullets, most important first.
Bullet 2: 'Session API breaks in 6.0.'
Is that confirmed? The vendor changelog says 'possible'.

options.verdict: Shorter, but still no comparison view, and the hedge was compressed away.
options.why: Right pattern, wrong problem: ordering helps, but the issue is format by content type and lost characterisation. Compressing harder strips the hedging further.

options.text: Add a review subagent that rewrites the briefing for readability after synthesis, checking tone, clarity and consistency in each section.

trace.text: Review subagent polishes 140 bullets into consistent wording.
'Possible breaking change' becomes 'Breaking change' for consistency.
One more agent call per briefing; comparison still impossible.

options.verdict: More polish, more cost, and the uncertainty was edited out.
options.why: Over-engineered: another agent is added before the proportionate fix of rendering by content type. Rewriting for consistency actively erases source characterisations.

options.text: Render version and vulnerability comparisons as a table, migration context as prose and code findings as a list, keeping each source's own wording.
options.code:
## Version comparison
| Version | Fixes | Vulns closed | Severity (source, date) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5.2 | 41 | 3 | High (NVD, 2026-08) |
| 6.0 | 112 | 5 | Critical (NVD, 2026-09) |

## Migration notes
Prose summary of the upgrade path...

## Code findings
- 23 call sites use the removed legacy router (grep)
- Session API: "possible" breaking change (vendor changelog, 2026-09)

trace.text: Version data rendered as a 4-row comparison table with source and date.
Migration path written as two paragraphs of prose.
Code findings listed; session API change kept as 'possible (vendor changelog)'.
Picks 6.0 from the table in a minute and schedules a spike to confirm the session change.

options.verdict: Comparable at a glance, with each claim as certain as its source said.
options.why: Content should be rendered by type, such as tables for comparisons and lists for findings, rather than flattened. Keeping original characterisations separates confirmed facts from contested ones.

labs.takeaway: Render by content type and keep each source's own certainty; never flatten a report into one format.

checks.q: Why should subagents return structured claim-source mappings instead of short prose summaries?
checks.a: Prose compression drops which source said what. The synthesis step cannot reconstruct attribution that was never passed to it.

checks.q: Two sources give 12% and 18% for the same metric. What should you check before calling it a conflict?
checks.a: Their publication or collection dates and methods. The difference may reflect different time periods or samples rather than a contradiction.

checks.q: How should a report present financial comparisons versus news developments?
checks.a: Financial data as tables and news as prose, with technical findings as lists. Do not flatten everything into one format.

left.title: Concise prose summaries
items: No record of which source said what
No dates, so trends look like conflicts

right.title: Claim-source mappings
items: Claim, source, excerpt for every finding
Dates and methods kept with each claim

quiz.q: Two credible sources from the same period give 44% and 61% for the same metric. What should the report do?
options: Use the figure from the more reputable-sounding source
Show both values with attribution and mark it contested
Average them and report 52.5% as the best estimate
Leave the metric out because the sources do not agree
quiz.why: Silently choosing or blending hides a real disagreement. Both values should appear with their sources so readers can judge.

quiz.q: Subagents return claim-source mappings, but citations are missing from the final report. Where is the fix?
options: Make the synthesis step preserve and merge the mappings
Ask subagents for shorter summaries so synthesis is easier
Let synthesis add citations from its own general knowledge
Remove citations from contested claims to keep things clear
quiz.why: The mappings existed but synthesis rewrote them away. Synthesis must carry them through, not regenerate or drop them.

quiz.q: Who should decide how conflicting findings are reconciled, and when?
options: Each subagent, while it is still gathering its own findings
The reader, after the final report has been delivered
The synthesis step, as it writes each section of the report
The coordinator, before the synthesis step begins
quiz.why: The coordinator sees all findings together and decides how to handle conflicts before synthesis, so synthesis does not resolve them silently.

quiz.q: One survey covered only large firms; another covered all firms. Both report adoption rates. How should the report treat them?
options: Treat them as directly comparable figures for one metric
Keep only the survey with the larger total sample size
Keep each figure with its source and methodological context
Merge them into a single adoption figure for simplicity
quiz.why: Reports keep each source's original characterisation and method. Stripping that context makes incomparable numbers look comparable.

misconceptions.myth: A stronger synthesis prompt can bring back lost citations.
misconceptions.fact: If subagents never passed claim-source mappings, there is nothing to cite. Attribution must be carried from the start.

misconceptions.myth: Two different figures for the same metric mean one source is wrong.
misconceptions.fact: Check dates and methodology first. The difference may be a trend or a different sample.

misconceptions.myth: Uniform bullet points make a report more consistent and clear.
misconceptions.fact: Different content reads best in different formats: tables for financial data, prose for news, lists for technical findings.

scenario.title: Multi-Agent Research System
scenario.story:
A strategy team used a multi-agent system to size the UK market for cloud accounting among small firms. The board report said, simply, '61% of UK SMEs use cloud accounting.' The board approved a plan on that basis.

A month later an analyst found that a second subagent had reported **44%** from an independent survey. The synthesis prompt had said 'where numbers conflict, use the most plausible one'. Worse, the 61% came from a vendor panel of existing software customers only, and that detail had been lost.

The team changed the subagent output to **claim-source mappings**: claim, value, source URL, excerpt, publication date and methodology. The coordinator now checks for conflicts before synthesis and decides how to present them. Synthesis must keep every mapping. The revised report showed both figures in a table, with dates and sample notes, and marked adoption as 'contested'. Settled findings were labelled 'well established'. The board re-sized the plan on a range and commissioned one more independent source.
